1.pericope_label: The command to consecrate Aaron and his sons

schools.summary: Gill rejects Jarchi's dating of this paragraph to a week before the tabernacle went up, arguing that the preceding chapters were spoken out of the tabernacle and so presuppose it standing, and that the order was renewed once the sacrificial laws had been given so that the new priests might have something to offer; he also treats the record itself as evidence that Moses acted under warrant rather than family feeling. Calvin goes further and moves his own treatment of the execution to the dedication of the tabernacle, so that the history may run uninterrupted, and adds a note on the priest's meal offering — a cake fried in a pan and wholly burnt, since had it been kept for his use, as the people's remainder was, it might easily have become an occasion of vain ostentation.

Henry gives the reasons for the delay in homelier terms: a tabernacle without priests would be a candlestick without a candle, and a law of sacrifice could not be kept without them, yet consecration had to wait until the place of ministry was ready, so that the men might set to work the moment they were ordained and understand that they were ordained not merely to honour and profit but to the business of the priesthood. He also notices the delicacy of Moses consecrating his own relations, and why he would not do it without further orders.
Clarke marks the distinction briefly: until now the thing had only been commanded, and here it is first performed.

Ellicott explains the placement — the rite required several kinds of offering, so each ritual had to be defined first, after which the lawgiver resumes the narrative broken off at the close of Exodus — and corrects the article in the list of materials, reading the bullock, the two rams and the basket, the very offering prescribed in Exodus. Keil and Delitzsch put the same point structurally and sketch the three stages that follow: consecration by investiture, anointing and sacrifice; entrance upon office; and the sanctifying of the priesthood by judgment on Aaron's eldest sons.

debates: When this paragraph was spoken. Jarchi placed it a week before the tabernacle was set up; Gill rejects that, since the preceding chapters were spoken out of the tabernacle; and Calvin, holding that the execution belongs to the day of the tabernacle's dedication, transfers his own exposition to that place rather than treat it here.
themes: the priest as minister for others

3.pericope_label: The assembly gathered at the entrance

schools.summary: Gill takes the summons, on Aben Ezra's reading, for the heads of the tribes and the elders, since every individual could not be got together, has Moses come bringing the garments, the oil and the sacrifices, and notes that when he spoke he opened the reason for the gathering not of himself but by divine direction. Calvin explains why he handles this material here rather than under the Second Commandment, where he expounded the priesthood's nature: these chapters are historical, and keeping them apart lets the reader see how faithfully Moses performed what he was commanded. He adds that many passages make it plain the priests were anointed on the same day the tabernacle was consecrated.

Wesley allows a larger crowd than the elders alone: they represented everyone, but as many of the people as wished and could reach the place came too, so that all might witness both Aaron's commission from God and the work it committed him to.

Ellicott would render the word assembly rather than congregation and identifies it with the elders and principal men, confirming the reading from the next chapter, where those same elders are called the children of Israel because they stood for them; he corrects the venue to the entrance of the tent of meeting, meaning its courtyard, pictures the overflow standing on ground that overlooked the enclosure, and reports a tradition current in the time of Christ which dated the ceremony to the twenty-third of Adar.

Gill locates the washing at the laver in the court, describes the linen coat as lying next the flesh and the garments as going on in exactly the order the text gives, explains that the linen drawers are missing from the list because it would not have been decent to have them put on before the whole assembly, and gives the breastplate as made of the same materials as the ephod and fastened to it.
Clarke notes that the Urim and the Thummim are here supposed to be something different from the breastplate itself.

Ellicott establishes philologically that washing with water, where no part of the body is named, means bathing the whole of it, places the act behind a curtain rather than before the people, and adds from later practice that under the second Temple the immersion required a hollow cut in the ground holding at least twenty-four cubic feet of water, the installation itself passing from Moses to the Sanhedrin who sat in his seat. He separates two things the English blurs — the needlework belt that girded the tunic and the band woven out of the same piece as the ephod — describes the ephod and the seamless blue robe, and reads the verb at the breastplate as putting the Urim and Thummim into its bag. Keil and Delitzsch supply the meaning of the whole operation: an official dress of that importance signified endowment with the character the office required, the costume being the outward sign of installation.

10.pericope_label: The anointing of the sanctuary and the priest

schools.summary: Gill notes that Bezaleel compounded the oil on directions Moses had from the Lord, reports Jarchi's frank admission that he does not know how the sevenfold sprinkling was ordered, and suggests the number marks a perfect unction making the altar a fitter type of Christ; on Aaron he traces the oil down to the beard and the collar of the robe, correcting the English which has it reach the skirts of his garments. Calvin explains why oil at all — without the Spirit's influence every sacrifice would be unsavoury, and it was by that same Spirit that Christ was made peace-maker — reads the laying on of hands as a testimony that guilt had been transferred to the victim, and treats the question why only the right side was consecrated as worth raising and not worth pressing, warning against wanting to know more than Scripture reveals; the ear rather than the tongue he explains from the office, which was to intercession and not to teaching, obedience being the chief virtue that obtains grace in sacrifice.

Wesley marks the difference in treatment: where the furniture was sprinkled, the oil was poured on the high priest plentifully, because his unction typified the anointing of Christ with a Spirit not given him by measure, of which every believer receives a measure.

Ellicott lists what the oil touched and defines the sanctifying as separation from common use, confirms that the sevenfold sprinkling is absent from the Exodus directions, and draws out the altar's new standing as itself sanctifying what was offered on it. He distinguishes the profuse pouring reserved for every successor to the high-priesthood from the simple marking of ordinary priests on the forehead. Keil and Delitzsch note that the victims were provided by Moses at the congregation's charge, and that Moses, as mediator of the covenant, performed every part of the rite himself.

debates: What figure was drawn on the high priest's forehead after the oil was poured. Jarchi and Maimonides describe the anointer drawing it between the eyebrows in the shape of a Greek chi; the practice Ellicott reports from the second Temple made the figure a Caph, the initial letter of the word for priest.
themes: the altar that sanctifies the gift

14.pericope_label: The bullock of the sin offering

schools.summary: Gill points out that neither Aaron nor his sons could kill the beast, not being fully consecrated, so Moses did it; he identifies the fat on the inwards by its anatomical name, and reports Aben Ezra's two opinions about the burning outside the camp — that Moses did it, or that he gave the order, which Gill thinks likelier.

Henry explains why a consecration needs victims: the covenant of priesthood, like other covenants, had to be made by sacrifice, and so Christ was consecrated by the sacrifice of himself. He finds a pastoral reason in the offerings made for the priests themselves — men who had stood beside their own sin offering would afterwards present the people's gifts with more tenderness, having compassion on the ignorant rather than insulting over them — and concludes that ministers who declare pardon to others should be diligent to have their own sins pardoned first.

Clarke states that the sin offering was repeated on each of the seven days of consecration; Wesley reconciles that with a text naming only one bullock by observing that Moses is describing the first day's work alone, and notices that the hide, which in offerings made for the people went to the priest, was here burnt.

Ellicott makes the ceremony's logic explicit — duly consecrated though they were, Aaron and his sons had to be purged before beginning priestly work, so they stood beside the victim as penitent sinners while Moses acted as delegated mediator — has him catch the blood in a bowl and throw it on the four corners rather than the horns of the incense altar, and explains why nobody ate the flesh. Keil and Delitzsch note the rank of the animal, a young ox answering to the priests' standing as the elect of the covenant nation, and explain the departure from the usual rule: the blood stayed on the brazen altar rather than entering the sanctuary in order to make this sin offering a consecration sacrifice.

debates: Whether one bullock was offered or seven. Clarke states that the sin offering was repeated on each of the seven days; Wesley accounts for the single animal named in the text by observing that Moses is describing only the work of the first day.

18.pericope_label: The ram of the burnt offering

schools.summary: Gill notes that the ram was one of the two Moses had been told to take, has Moses kill it on the Greek version's authority, and follows the butchery through — the head struck off and the carcase quartered, the inwards drawn and the legs severed and washed.

Wesley reads the offering as the new priests giving God the glory of the honour just put upon them and devoting themselves and all their service to him, and leaves room for a deputy at the killing: the verb may mean Moses, as the following clause certainly does, or some other person acting by his appointment — a vagueness he explains by the text naming Moses expressly for the sprinkling of the blood, an act more properly priestly and more essential to the sacrifice.

Ellicott fixes the sequence, the burnt offering following the expiation of their sins by the sin offering, notes that the ritual otherwise follows the ordinary rules except that Moses performed the priestly acts himself, and catches a distinction the English loses, since the word here is not the one used at the sin offering and is better rendered cast than sprinkled. Keil and Delitzsch mark the transition, the sin offering having removed every disturbance of fellowship caused by the sin of the very men being installed.

22.pericope_label: The ram of consecration; blood on ear, thumb and toe

schools.summary: Gill renders the name filling, or fulnesses, and reports Jarchi's explanation that these offerings filled and perfected the priests in their priesthood, this being the finishing and consummation of the whole consecration.

Clarke goes outside Scripture for his comment, following Calmet in setting beside this rite the making of a Roman high priest — robed in silk and crowned with gold, led down into a pit roofed with pierced planks, and drenched from head to tongue in the blood of a bullock killed above him, coming up to be adored as supreme pontiff. He quotes Prudentius at length for the details, and judges the direction of borrowing to run from Aaron to Rome rather than the reverse.

Ellicott describes the concluding sacrifice as resembling in form both thank offering and peace offering and as expressing the gratitude Aaron and his sons felt at their appointment, together with their peace and fellowship with God; he reads the blood on the tip of the right ear as teaching the mediator to hearken to God's commandments and the blood on the right thumb as reminding him to execute them, explains the choice of the right side by its being the stronger, notes that a cured leper had the same members touched, and corrects the fat and the rump to the fat and the fat-tail. Keil and Delitzsch derive the title from the ceremony performed with the flesh, by which the sacrifice inducted these men into possession of the priestly privileges.

outliers: Clarke's comparison of the consecration with the Roman taurobolium runs the opposite way from what a reader might expect. He does not treat the Hebrew rite as a variant of the pagan one but judges the Roman ceremony to bear a striking allusion to Aaron's consecration, to have probably been borrowed from it, and then to have been disguised by the introduction of Rome's own superstitions.

26.pericope_label: The wave offering; oil and blood sprinkled

schools.summary: Gill has Moses take the unleavened bread from the basket, lay it with the fat and the right shoulder on the hands of Aaron and his sons, and take the whole back once it had been waved; on the closing act he notices that the oil and the blood from the altar seem to have been combined, the wording running them together.

Clarke refers the nature of the waving and heaving to his fuller treatment in Exodus, and fastens on the sprinkling of the high priest himself as a type discharged in Christ, who was sprinkled with his own blood in the agony of the garden, in the crowning with thorns, in the piercing of hands and feet, and in the opening of his side — four acts of atonement performed by the high priest himself. Wesley states the principle behind the breast-piece bluntly: Moses was administering the priest's office at the time, and was therefore to receive the priest's wages.

Ellicott explains that the breast-piece, afterwards the perquisite of whichever priest officiated, fell here to Moses as the man divinely appointed to perform the service, and observes that the sacred garments received the same cleansing and sanctification as the men who wore them, the vestments being the badge of the office — which lies behind the apostle's remark that almost all things are by the law purged with blood.

debates: Whether the anointing oil and the blood were mixed before being sprinkled. Gill takes the wording to run them together and supposes they were combined; Ellicott holds that whether they were sprinkled separately or mingled first cannot possibly be gathered either from this verse or from the passage in Exodus which prescribes the rite.

schools.summary: Gill grows practical about how literally the confinement was meant: Jewish writers are puzzled where the men were to relieve themselves, the place being holy, and he answers that the order cannot have forbidden going in and out at all, only lingering or attending other business, since some had always to be on the spot in turns and they must have slept alternately. Calvin calls the rest of the ritual the universal rule and singles the week out as the one special thing — God kept them in the tabernacle so that they might learn to subordinate every domestic care and worldly business to their sacred duties, the number reminding them that for the rest of their lives they were no longer their own masters.

Henry reads the meal as their thankful consent to the consecration, comparing Ezekiel, who at his commission was told to eat the roll; gets a soldier's lesson from the week indoors, the priesthood being a good warfare in which men must learn to endure hardness and disentangle themselves from the affairs of this life; and finds doctrine in the repetition, since it shows the imperfection of legal sacrifices, repeated because they could not take away sin and repeated seven times because they typified the one offering that perfected for ever those who are sanctified. On the charge itself he presses hardest: every one of us has a charge to keep, and it is death, eternal death, to betray the trust we are charged with.

Clarke takes seven as the Hebrew number of perfection, so that the week implies a perfect and full consecration. Wesley notes that Moses handed his own portion to Aaron in token that the priests alone should have that right in future, and leaves open whether the he who consecrates is God or Moses, since Moses often speaks of himself in the third person.

Ellicott specifies what was left for the sacrificial meal, corrects the venue to the entrance of the tent of meeting, and names the two features distinguishing this meal from an ordinary peace offering — it had to be eaten with unleavened bread, and no layman could share it, the flesh and bread being peculiarly holy. He also spells out what the daily repetition involved: sin offering, burnt offering and consecration offering each day, with the men and their garments sprinkled afresh. Keil and Delitzsch take the words to imply that the rite in all its details was performed again for seven days.

themes: repeated sacrifices and the one offering

34.pericope_label: So Aaron and his sons did all

schools.summary: Gill has the whole ceremony performed again on each remaining day, citing Jarchi and Aben Ezra, and reports a rabbinic gloss referring the verb in the preceding clause to the business of the red heifer; on where the men were to stay he prefers Noldius's rendering within rather than at, since they were forbidden to go out of the door at all, and sums up their obedience in a sentence — they submitted to have done to them and for them on every remaining day what had been done on the first, and kept inside the whole time.

Clarke reads the closing verse as a receipt for the exact fulfilment of the commands delivered in Exodus, quotes Ainsworth at length on a priesthood that was a covenant of life and peace yet made without an oath, needing many priests because death would not suffer them to continue and offering gifts that could not perfect the conscience, until Christ came as priest with an oath and surety of a better covenant; and he closes with the sharpest statement of the chapter's logic, that taken in reference to Christ's priesthood these rites are significant and edifying but taken out of that relation would be as absurd and nugatory as the making of a Roman pontiff. Wesley makes the same contrast briefly, reserving one point for the honour of Christ's priesthood — they were made priests without an oath, but Christ with an oath.

Ellicott improves the rendering to as hath been done this day rather than as he hath done, and states the sense plainly: the rites gone through on the first day the Lord commanded to be repeated every day for a week.
